modules.title: Encounter, Detention & Probable Cause
modules.intro: A consensual contact allows questions without compelled answers. A seizure requires legal justification. Reasonable suspicion permits a limited investigative detention; probable cause is a higher threshold and must be linked to the suspected offense.
modules.caseText: Repeated casing-like conduct supported a brief stop; an additional safety basis supported a limited frisk. A stop does not authorize an automatic search.
modules.takeaway: Articulate the exact facts known when the person was seized; distinguish the basis for the stop from the basis for a frisk.

scenarios.q: An officer politely asks a pedestrian for directions and does not block departure. The pedestrian walks away.
a: Allow departure absent independent grounds
Detain for refusing to answer
Search for identification
scenarios.why: Refusal to participate in a consensual encounter alone does not establish reasonable suspicion.

scenarios.q: A person matches a detailed recent robbery description near the scene and takes evasive action when officers arrive.
a: Automatic custodial arrest
Briefly detain if the totality supports reasonable suspicion
Search the person's phone
scenarios.why: Evaluate particularized facts and duration; reasonable suspicion is not automatically probable cause.

scenarios.q: During a justified stop, the person keeps reaching toward a concealed waistband despite warnings and the officer can articulate a weapon concern.
a: Limited protective frisk for weapons if armed-and-dangerous suspicion exists
Search every container for evidence
Arrest solely for nervousness
scenarios.why: A protective frisk is safety-limited, not a general evidence search.

modules.title: Texas Warrantless Arrest Authority
modules.intro: First ask whether probable cause exists. Then identify the Texas law authorizing arrest without a warrant. CCP 14.01(b) covers offenses committed in the officer's presence or view. CCP 14.03 contains specific exceptions, including qualifying family violence, assault with danger of further injury, protective-order violations, and interference with an emergency telephone call. These are not blanket exceptions.
modules.case: Atwater v. City of Lago Vista, 532 U.S. 318 (2001)
modules.caseText: The Fourth Amendment permitted an arrest for a minor offense committed in the officer's presence, but state arrest authority and policy still require separate review.
modules.takeaway: State the factual basis for probable cause and the specific warrantless-arrest exception, or obtain a warrant.

scenarios.q: An officer develops probable cause for a reported misdemeanor criminal mischief from several weeks ago; no exception applies.
a: Seek a warrant
Arrest because probable cause is always enough
Arrest because the suspect is cooperative
scenarios.why: For a past misdemeanor not witnessed and without an exception, probable cause alone does not authorize warrantless arrest.

scenarios.q: An officer has probable cause that a suspect committed an offense involving family violence outside the officer's presence.
a: Consider the family-violence warrantless-arrest exception and its conditions
Never arrest without witnessing it
Treat all domestic arguments as crimes
scenarios.why: CCP 14.03(a)(4) addresses an offense involving family violence; verify the offense, family-violence facts and applicable conditions.

scenarios.q: An officer has probable cause for interference with an emergency telephone call during an emergency, not personally witnessed.
a: Consider the specific emergency-call warrantless-arrest exception
Only arrest if a dispatcher witnessed it
No arrest authority ever exists
scenarios.why: CCP 14.03(a)(5) provides a specific exception; verify Penal Code 42.062 elements and current statutory text.

scenarios.q: A reported assault caused bodily injury; there is also probable cause the suspect presents danger of further bodily injury to the victim.
a: Consider the assault-and-further-danger exception
An assault report alone always permits arrest
Arrest only if officer witnessed the assault
scenarios.why: CCP 14.03(a)(2) requires both assault causing bodily injury and danger of further bodily injury.

scenarios.q: An officer has probable cause of a qualifying protective-order violation outside the officer's presence.
a: Consider the qualifying protective-order exception
All protective-order disputes mandate arrest
No warrantless exception exists
scenarios.why: CCP 14.03(a)(3) applies to qualifying Penal Code 25.07 violations; verify order and offense elements.

modules.title: Frisks, Consent & Searches of People
modules.intro: A Terry frisk requires reasonable suspicion the person is armed and dangerous and is limited to locating weapons. Consent must be voluntary and the search remain within its scope. An arrest does not justify an unlimited search of every nearby item.
modules.caseText: During a lawful frisk, the plain-feel doctrine is narrow; manipulation of an object beyond the protective purpose is not authorized.
modules.takeaway: Explain the separate basis and permitted scope for each search.

scenarios.q: A lawful detention is underway, but the officer has no facts indicating weapons.
a: Do not automatically frisk
Frisk everyone during every detention
Search pockets for contraband
scenarios.why: A detention alone does not authorize a frisk.

scenarios.q: A person voluntarily consents to a search of a backpack but expressly excludes a zipped personal pouch.
a: Respect the expressed limitation absent another lawful basis
Ignore the limitation
Treat consent as irrevocable permission for all property
scenarios.why: Consent searches are limited by objective scope and may be restricted or withdrawn.

scenarios.q: During a lawful weapons frisk, an officer feels an object that is clearly not a weapon and squeezes it to determine if it is drugs.
a: Stop manipulation unless another lawful basis exists
Manipulate freely to identify contraband
Automatically arrest
scenarios.why: Dickerson limits plain feel and prohibits exceeding the weapons frisk's lawful scope.

modules.title: Vehicles & Traffic Stops
modules.intro: A traffic stop is a seizure. Its duration must relate to the traffic mission and lawful safety tasks unless separate reasonable suspicion justifies prolongation. Vehicle searches require a valid exception: consent, probable cause under the automobile exception, a properly justified inventory, or a limited search incident to arrest under Gant.
modules.case: Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015); Arizona v. Gant, 556 U.S. 332 (2009)
modules.caseText: Rodriguez restricts prolonging a traffic stop for unrelated investigation without separate reasonable suspicion. Gant restricts vehicle searches incident to arrest.
modules.takeaway: Name the search exception and identify the facts supporting it before opening a vehicle compartment.

scenarios.q: A traffic citation is complete; an officer extends the stop solely to await a dog without independent reasonable suspicion.
a: Do not prolong the stop for that purpose
Extend indefinitely
Search automatically
scenarios.why: Rodriguez requires independent justification for an unrelated extension.

scenarios.q: A driver is arrested for a license offense and secured in a patrol car; there is no reason to believe offense evidence is in the car.
a: Do not automatically search incident to arrest
Search any compartment automatically
Search because an arrest occurred
scenarios.why: Gant's vehicle search-incident framework does not permit an automatic search on these facts.

scenarios.q: An officer develops probable cause that a vehicle contains contraband and the automobile exception applies.
a: Search areas where the object of the search may reasonably be found
Search only the driver's seat
Search the owner's home too
scenarios.why: The automobile exception has an object-and-location scope; it does not authorize a home search.

modules.title: Homes, Warrants & Exigency
modules.intro: Entry into a home ordinarily requires a warrant or a recognized exception. Consent requires authority and voluntariness; exigency must be supported by concrete facts. An arrest warrant for one person does not automatically authorize entering a third party's home.
modules.case: Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980); Steagald v. United States, 451 U.S. 204 (1981)
modules.caseText: Payton protects the home against routine warrantless entry to arrest. Steagald distinguishes an arrest warrant from authority to enter a third party's home.
modules.takeaway: Before crossing a threshold, identify the warrant or exception and the premises to which it applies.

scenarios.q: Officers have probable cause of a misdemeanor but no warrant, consent, or exigency; suspect is inside a residence.
a: Seek judicial authorization rather than enter
Enter solely because probable cause exists
Treat the front door as public
scenarios.why: Home entry needs its own legal justification.

scenarios.q: A person with apparent common authority voluntarily allows entry to shared living areas.
a: Evaluate authority, voluntariness and scope
Assume consent covers all private locked spaces
Ignore an objecting physically present co-occupant
scenarios.why: Consent authority and scope are fact-specific; occupant objections can change the analysis.

scenarios.q: Officers hold an arrest warrant for a suspect believed to be visiting someone else's residence.
a: Assess need for a search warrant or valid exception to enter the third party's home
Use the arrest warrant as universal entry authority
Enter without checking location
scenarios.why: Steagald recognizes independent privacy interests of third-party occupants.

modules.title: Search Incident, Inventory & Evidence
modules.intro: Search incident to lawful custodial arrest has boundaries tied to the arrestee and the circumstances. Inventory is an administrative caretaking process performed under standardized policy, not a pretext for an investigative rummage. Plain view requires lawful vantage and lawful access.
modules.case: Chimel v. California, 395 U.S. 752 (1969); South Dakota v. Opperman, 428 U.S. 364 (1976)
modules.caseText: Chimel limits a search incident to arrest to the person and immediately accessible area. Opperman recognizes standardized vehicle inventories under appropriate circumstances.
modules.takeaway: Document the actual exception, standardized procedures when applicable, and the search scope.

scenarios.q: A vehicle is lawfully impounded; department policy specifies an inventory procedure.
a: Follow the standardized inventory procedure for caretaking purposes
Invent a broader procedure at the scene
Call every investigative search an inventory
scenarios.why: Inventory must be tied to lawful custody and standardized procedures.

scenarios.q: An officer lawfully observes contraband through an open doorway but has no lawful right to enter the home.
a: Obtain lawful access before seizing it
Enter because visibility alone authorizes entry
Ignore the entry issue
scenarios.why: Plain view does not eliminate the need for lawful access.

scenarios.q: After an arrest, an officer wants to search an unrelated locked room far from the secured arrestee.
a: Identify a separate lawful search basis
Search it automatically incident to arrest
Assume arrest makes the entire building searchable
scenarios.why: Chimel does not authorize searching remote areas merely because an arrest occurred.

modules.title: Miranda, Custody & Questioning
modules.intro: Miranda warnings are generally required before custodial interrogation, not for every encounter or arrest. Custody and interrogation are distinct inquiries. Volunteered statements are not necessarily the product of interrogation; invocation and waiver rules must be followed.
modules.case: Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966); Berkemer v. McCarty, 468 U.S. 420 (1984)
modules.caseText: Miranda addresses custodial interrogation. Berkemer explains that ordinary roadside traffic questioning is generally not automatically Miranda custody.
modules.takeaway: Ask separately: Is the person in custody for Miranda purposes? Is the officer interrogating?

scenarios.q: During an ordinary traffic stop, an officer asks routine questions without arrest-like restraints.
a: Analyze custody; Miranda is not automatically required solely because of a stop
Miranda is always required before any question
Every traffic stop is custodial interrogation
scenarios.why: Berkemer distinguishes typical roadside detention from Miranda custody.

scenarios.q: A handcuffed arrestee in an interview room is asked questions reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.
a: Provide Miranda warnings and obtain a valid waiver before custodial interrogation
No warnings needed because handcuffs are common
A report form substitutes for warnings
scenarios.why: Custody plus interrogation triggers Miranda protections absent an applicable exception.

scenarios.q: A person spontaneously blurts out an incriminating statement without prompting.
a: Document the voluntary statement and circumstances
Assume it is always inadmissible
Treat every spontaneous statement as an interrogation response
scenarios.why: Miranda generally addresses statements produced by custodial interrogation.

bank.q: Which fact best supports a detention?
a: Specific conduct linked to a suspected offense
A vague feeling
Refusal to chat alone
bank.why: Reasonable suspicion requires particularized objective facts.

bank.q: Probable cause to arrest and authority for a warrantless arrest are:
a: Irrelevant for misdemeanors
Separate legal questions
Always identical
bank.why: Texas statutory restrictions may apply independently.

bank.q: What does a person's refusal of a voluntary request generally establish by itself?
a: Probable cause
A frisk basis
No automatic reasonable suspicion
bank.why: Refusal alone ordinarily does not justify seizure.

bank.q: When is a frisk justified during a lawful stop?
a: Reasonable suspicion the person is armed and dangerous
Every time a stop is lawful
Only after a warrant
bank.why: Terry's frisk threshold is distinct.

bank.q: What is the proper purpose of a Terry frisk?
a: Inventorying belongings
Officer safety by locating weapons
A general search for evidence
bank.why: Protective frisks are limited.

bank.q: Which is a key condition of valid consent?
a: Written signature in every case
Probable cause
Voluntariness
bank.why: Voluntariness is assessed under the circumstances.

bank.q: If a person limits the scope of consent, an officer should:
a: Honor the limitation absent another exception
Ignore it
Treat consent as permanent
bank.why: Scope matters.

bank.q: When reviewing a delayed misdemeanor arrest, officers should:
a: Assume every report counts as presence
Identify a Chapter 14 exception or obtain a warrant
Rely on probable cause alone
bank.why: Probable cause alone is insufficient for every warrantless misdemeanor arrest.

bank.q: For the assault-bodily-injury warrantless exception, what extra factor matters?
a: The officer's preferred booking time
A signed confession
Probable cause of danger of further bodily injury
bank.why: CCP 14.03(a)(2) contains a further-danger condition.

bank.q: Which offense has a specifically identified warrantless-arrest exception in CCP 14.03?
a: Interference with an emergency telephone call
Every property misdemeanor
Any municipal code violation
bank.why: The statutory exception is specific and requires the offense elements.

bank.q: Does an arrest warrant always authorize entry into a third party's residence?
a: Only if officers are in uniform
No, separate entry authority may be needed
Yes, in every circumstance
bank.why: Steagald protects third-party premises.

bank.q: An inventory search should be:
a: A substitute for missing probable cause
Unlimited whenever a tow truck arrives
Consistent with standardized policy and lawful custody
bank.why: Inventory is administrative, not an evidence-search workaround.

bank.q: Under Gant, a vehicle search incident to arrest is:
a: Limited by specific conditions
Automatic whenever a driver is arrested
Always allowed after the vehicle is towed
bank.why: Gant limits this doctrine.

bank.q: What is needed to extend a completed traffic stop for an unrelated investigation?
a: An arrest warrant for the driver
Independent legal justification
Only officer curiosity
bank.why: Rodriguez addresses unrelated prolongation.

bank.q: Miranda generally becomes relevant when:
a: An officer asks any question
An officer starts a traffic stop
Custody and interrogation are both present
bank.why: Both custody and interrogation must be assessed.

bank.q: Plain view alone:
a: Does not eliminate the need for lawful access
Always permits forced entry
Authorizes a full house search
bank.why: Observation and physical access are separate questions.

bank.q: A useful arrest report should identify:
a: Facts discovered days afterward as if known earlier
Facts known at the time and the specific authority relied upon
Only the ultimate charge
bank.why: Chronology and contemporaneous facts matter.
